Hi everyone, my name is Justin, and along with some other people like @Marco David , we are trying to formalize A-infinity Categories in Lean. We have a general roadmap that looks like Graded Quivers -> AinfinityCategoryStruct -> AinfintiyCategory just like how Mathlib has Quiver -> CategoryStruct -> Category.

We already have a lot of lean code written, partially with the use of AI but under rigorous scrutiny and guidance, and hope to slowly add them to Mathlib. For the first milestone of defining Graded Quivers, our current code looks something like this:

module

public import Mathlib

@[expose] public section

open ChainComplex CategoryTheory DirectSum GradedMonoid GradedObject

namespace AInfinityTheory

universe u v w

/-- A grading index is an additive commutative group with a distinguished unit
element, together with a parity map to `ZMod 2`. The distinguished unit is used
to realize integer degree shifts via the canonical map `ℤ →+ β`. -/
class GradingIndex (β : Type u) extends AddCommGroupWithOne β where
  protected parity : β →+ ZMod 2
  protected parity_one : parity 1 = 1

/-- The parity homomorphism attached to a grading index. -/
def parity {β : Type u} [GradingIndex β] : β →+ ZMod 2 :=
  GradingIndex.parity

/-- The canonical additive homomorphism from `ℤ` into a grading index. -/
def GradingIndex.ofInt {β : Type u} [GradingIndex β] : ℤ →+ β :=
  Int.castAddHom β

/-- The parity of the distinguished unit is odd. -/
@[simp]
theorem parity_one {β : Type u} [GradingIndex β] : parity (1 : β) = 1 :=
  GradingIndex.parity_one

/-- The parity map agrees with integer casts modulo `2`. -/
@[simp]
theorem parity_intCast {β : Type u} [GradingIndex β] (n : ℤ) :
    parity (n : β) = (n : ZMod 2) := by
  rw [← zsmul_one n, map_zsmul, parity_one, zsmul_one]

/-- The canonical degree shift by an integer. Keeping this wrapper makes degree
formulas read naturally throughout the project. -/
def shift_ofInt {β} [GradingIndex β] (n : ℤ) : β :=
  GradingIndex.ofInt n

variable (β : Type v) [GradingIndex β]

abbrev GradedRModule (R : Type u) [CommRing R] :=
  GradedObject β (ModuleCat.{u} R)

/-- The graded R-module of morphisms between two objects. -/
class RLinearGQuiver (R : Type u) [CommRing R] (Obj : Type w) where
  protected GHom' : Obj → Obj → GradedRModule β R

def GHom (R : Type u) [CommRing R] {Obj : Type w} [RLinearGQuiver β R Obj] (X Y : Obj) : GradedRModule β R :=
  RLinearGQuiver.GHom' X Y

end AInfinityTheory

The above code is all self-contained. We are looking for feedback on our code, so please let me know your thoughts and potential improvements we can make.

The GradingIndex class is needed as in general we want to allow for grading by something other than the integers. The parity function is so that we can get a sign out of the grading. As in A-infinity Categories we will need signs like (-1)^|deg(x)|
Justin do you intend to use operads? (or are these the linear kind like here)
To every edge in the quiver should be assigned a (graded) R-module, so all our A∞ categories will be linear!
I hope this works out well. Do you think you would be able to formalize a "group-completion" operation like in 𝒦-theory?
In any case this is an exciting choice of project and I hope some other members check this out and comment ( I myself have not been involved in any PRs).

René Perry said:

I hope this works out well. Do you think you would be able to formalize a "group-completion" operation like in 𝒦-theory?

I don't think we will any time soon. Sorry

Does anyone have advice on how I would go about PRing this into Mathlib. And later a bunch more lean stuff on the roadmap Graded Quivers -> AinfinityCategoryStruct -> AinfintiyCategory. Any advice would be really appreciated
For reference, here is the blueprint homepage of the larger project that this development belongs to: https://marcodavid.net/a∞/

To give an idea of why we are defining all these objects, below I have attached the code for defining an AInfinityCategoryStruct

module

public import Mathlib
public import AInfinity.Grading

@[expose] public section

open CategoryTheory Finset AInfinityTheory

noncomputable section

namespace AInfinityTheory

universe u v w
variable {β : Type v} [GradingIndex β]
variable {n : ℕ}

/-- Target degree of the `n`-ary operation `m`. -/
abbrev operationTargetDeg
    (deg : Fin n → β) : β :=
  (∑ i, deg i) + shift_ofInt (2 - (n : ℤ))

/-- Target degree of the arity-`n` Stasheff relation. -/
abbrev stasheffTargetDeg
    (deg : Fin n → β) : β :=
  (∑ i, deg i) + shift_ofInt (3 - (n : ℤ))

/-- Valid index pairs for an arity-`n` Stasheff summand. -/
abbrev ValidStasheffIndices (n r s : ℕ) : Prop :=
  1 ≤ s ∧ r + s ≤ n

/-- The type of the `i`-th morphism in a composable string of objects and degrees. -/
abbrev ComposableHomType
    {R : Type u} [CommRing R]
    {Obj : Type w}
    (Hom : Obj → Obj → GradedRModule (β := β) (R := R))
    {n : ℕ}
    (obj : Fin (n + 1) → Obj)
    (deg : Fin n → β)
    (i : Fin n) : ModuleCat R :=
  Hom
    (obj ⟨i.val, Nat.lt_succ_of_lt i.isLt⟩)
    (obj ⟨i.val + 1, by omega⟩)
    (deg i)

/-- The target type of the `n`-ary operation on a composable string. -/
abbrev operationTargetType
    {R : Type u} [CommRing R]
    {Obj : Type w}
    (Hom : Obj → Obj → GradedRModule (β := β) (R := R))
    {n : ℕ}
    (obj : Fin (n + 1) → Obj)
    (deg : Fin n → β) : ModuleCat R :=
  Hom (obj 0) (obj (Fin.last n)) (operationTargetDeg deg)


class AInfinityCategoryStruct
    (R : Type u) [CommRing R] (Obj : Type w)
    extends RLinearGQuiver (β := β) R Obj where
  m :
    {n : ℕ} → [NeZero n] →
    (obj : Fin (n + 1) → Obj) →
    (deg : Fin n → β) →
    MultilinearMap R
      (fun i : Fin n => ComposableHomType (GHom β R) obj deg i)
      (operationTargetType (GHom β R) obj deg)

end AInfinityTheory

Please let me know if you have any comments. We are looking for feedback!

This seems like a very cool project! I don't understand much about A-infinity categories myself, but what Marco told me after ITP last year sounded very interesting.

Right now it seems like you've mostly been making new definitions without proving things about them. I think it's hard to say if a definition works well without also formalising some non-trivial proofs.

As you prove things you might want to make changes to your definitions. In this case it could actually be advantageous if the definition is still in your own project and not already upstreamed to Mathlib, because then you can make changes faster without going through the Mathlib PR review process (again). However, you will probably find various small API lemmas that are currently missing from the library and those would probably be very much appreciated in Mathlib PRs.

Since I'm not very familiar with A-infinity category theory I find it hard to give concrete feedback on your code, perhaps @Emily Riehl or @Steve Awodey can say more? (I hope it's okay that I ping you). In any case, I'm looking forward to hearing more about how this project will go!

@Jonas Bayer We have developed a decent amount of code so far. Although we have not proved that many things, we have constructed some examples using our definitions and proved basic things, such as the composition of A-infinity functors is associative.

We are looking both for feedback on our design choices at a high-level but also just general Lean improvements. Any feedback would be great!

From the blueprint it seems that there are only two (unproven) lemmas and lots of definitions in the project. But having looked at the repo I can see that you've also done some simple proofs.

What is your motivation behind defining computable binary biproducts? Does this make the formalisation nicer anywhere? In Mathlib, as far as I can tell, it is often fine for things to be not computable.

Minor code style feedback/recommendations:

  • I'd always use Type* unless explicit universe variables are actually necessary
  • You can type #min_imports at the end of a file which shows you just what you need so you don't need to import all of Mathlib
  • There seems to be a lot of use of abbrev in the project, even for complicated definitions. I think it might be better to always use def unless you have a good reason for the definition to always be unfolded.
  • I saw that you used AInfinityCategory (β := β) R Obj -- probably you want to make β\betaβ explicit instead.
  • shift_ofInt should be shiftOfInt if you follow Mathlib naming conventions (and maybe you don't actually need this definition and could just use Grading.ofInt)

Also note that people on this Zulip don't like to give feedback on LLM written code (since it's a lot of effort and it's often unclear if the person who posted the code will learn from it). I believe that you were careful when using AI in your project, but maybe in the future it would be better to ask for feedback only for code that is entirely human-written.

@Jonas Bayer The A-infinity categories part has nothing to do with binary biproducts, someone else worked on that so I am not sure about that part.

A lot of the abbrevs in the project are just for convenience but you do have a fair point that we should change most of them to def. I'm not too sure about whether beta should be explicit, maybe @Niels Voss could talk a little more about that.

We are very careful about using AI in our lean code. All of our definitions are constructed by us, we just sometimes leave the helper lemmas that need to be proven to AI. Thanks for all your feedback!

The computable biproducts is somewhat unrelated. The project right now is split into two (currently) non-interacting parts which will be connected later: A-infinity categories, and KLRW computation. A construction in symplectic geometry is captured algebraically by cochain complexes on some suitable completion of the KLRW category on the A1A_1A1​ dynkin diagram (you can ask @Marco David for details).

Up to quasi-isomorphism, the braid group B⁡n\operatorname{B}_nBn​ acts as an A∞A_{\infty}A∞​-endofunctor on the category K⁡∙(Add(KLRWn)⁡)\operatorname{K}^{\bullet}(\operatorname{Add(KLRW_n)})K∙(Add(KLRWn​)) of bounded cochain complexes of the additive completion of the KLRW category of the A1A_1A1​ quiver on nnn strands. This gives a very strong braid-group invariant. In addition to proving this is well-defined, we actually want to use it to do real computations, which means we need to use computable constructions for this half of the project. Mathlib was already over 80% of the way to having all of the ingredients be computable, so we just needed to construct computable versions of docs#CategoryTheory.Mat_ (the additive completion), docs#CategoryTheory.Limits.HasZeroObject, and docs#CategoryTheory.Limits.HasBinaryBiproducts and make a bounded version of docs#CochainComplex.

First of all let me say that as someone working with A-infinity categories, I very much look forward to the development in this project.
A first question I have is how you deal with the different sign conventions in the area? There are at least 3 major ones and if one would like to upstream to mathlib one would either have to decide on one (with good reasons) or treat all at the same time (with appropriate interaction).
Regarding suggestions for basic lemmas/theorems that should (in my opinion) be proved to ensure that the basic setup is meaningful, here are some that come to mind: 1) a dg category is precisely an A-infinity category with vanishing higher multiplications. 2) the bar construction. 3) every A-infinity category has a dg category model. 4) every A-infinity category has a minimal model, or more general Kadeishvili's theorem/homological perturbation. 5) structure transport, aka formal diffeomorphisms of A-infinity categories. 6) Verification of some basic A-infinity-structures e.g. the one on

Ext⁡k[x]/xn∗(k,k)\operatorname{Ext}_{k[x]/x^n}^*(k,k)Extk[x]/xn∗​(k,k)

For sign conventions, surely the thing to do is to (a) choose one (b) document it very clearly, explaining the differences between your choice and the choices in various other canonical sources. This is what we did, for example, for defining the shift functor on complexes (the issue there was whether the differentials changed sign, which they do in some sources but not others; we made one choice and then added appropriate signs to deal with the others)

@Julian Külshammer All the code we have written so far follows the sign conventions used in symplectic geometry, namely, we are following the signs in Seidel's textbook. I know of the other sign convention used by Keller. What was the third sign convention you had in mind? Do you have any opinions on which one should be chosen? Personally, I think the symplectic geometry sign convention is the simplest of the bunch. We can certainly prove the equivalence of all the sign conventions sometime later in Lean.

I don't think dg-categories have been implemented in Mathlib, although, as you mentioned, the definition of A-infinity categories generalizes them. I agree that many of these constructions and theorems should be made in Lean. Although some things, like the minimal model theorem, would probably take considerable effort to prove.

Thanks for the feedback. We are trying to get the PR process started for Mathlib, as it is known to take a long time and this way we can get early feedback on our Lean code.

In my experience (albeit in another area) it is sometimes too much to hope for the "right" sign convention in mathematics. One particularly bad situation I see in number theory is a sign choice where people working in one area prefer a +, and people working in another area choose a -, and each choice is perfect for that area because it makes all the formulae come out nice, and it makes all the formulae in the other area have a random - sign in :-) Basically the issue is that homology is dual to cohomology, and the sign convention depends on whether you think homology or cohomology is the interesting object (and both are interesting, but for different reasons).

@Justin Mu Personally, I use the same sign convention as Keller. (Lefevre-Hasegawa uses a slightly different sign convention.) Personally, I don't understand the sign convention in symplectic geometry and I would definitely not call it the "simplest of the bunch". As an outsider, it seems to be the most adapted for examples coming from symplectic geometry (similar to the situation @Kevin Buzzard describes). For me a big disadvantage of these sign conventions is that with these is that an ordinary graded category is no longer an instance of an A-infinity category. One has to twist the multiplication and define m2(a,b)=(−1)∣b∣a∘bm_2(a,b)=(-1)^{|b|}a\circ bm2​(a,b)=(−1)∣b∣a∘b. Relatedly, (strict) unitality then has the strange convention that m2(a,1)=am_2(a,1)=am2​(a,1)=a and m2(1,b)=(−1)∣b∣bm_2(1,b)=(-1)^{|b|}bm2​(1,b)=(−1)∣b∣b. To me this would seem a strange choice for mathlib.

If I compare the development to what I remember from the development of homological algebra in Lean/Mathlib, it took some time to settle on conventions and trying to prove certain results enabled making choices and ensuring these choices would enable further development.

I know nothing about A-infinity categories, but about sign conventions, in order to obtain the monoidal category structure on categories of homological complexes https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Algebra/Homology/Monoidal.html I introduced typeclasses in https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Algebra/Homology/ComplexShapeSigns.html
In order to have good interactions between A-infinity/dg-categories with the existing API for homological complexes, it seems important to use the same API whenever it is possible.
@Joël Riou I think the application programming interface for this one should have some prerequisites.
Nevermind, I don't want to dampen the spirits (it just surprised me somewhat). I hope you make great progress on your endeavors here especially as it concerns the braid group.

Sorry for my inactivity in the past months, but I hope to continue this project.
Regarding the sign conventions, I think we can sort that later down the road as a lot has to be done first before that matters to much.

Hi everyone, I'm looking to start the process of PRing the lean code for A-infinity Categories that my team and I have been developing. In particular, the first PR would be defining Graded Quivers. The block of code for this is in the first message in this channel.
Does anyone have suggestions on how to go about PRing this? In particular, where should this go inside Mathlib, with regard to the file system?
I was thinking either Algebra/Homology or in CategoryTheory. This is my first time contributing code to Mathlib so I would like some guidance. Any feedback would be greatly appreciated.
